subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will compare things in new ways. You will say which object is heavier and which is lighter, use a balance scale and non-standard units, compare containers by how much they hold, compare length and height, and describe temperature as hot, warm or cold.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Compare two objects by mass and say which is heavier, lighter, or the same.
Understand that a balance scale tips down on the heavier side.
Compare containers by capacity: holds more, holds less, full, empty.
Use the words nearly full and nearly empty for in-between amounts.
Compare objects by length and height: longer, shorter, taller, same length.
Line objects up at one end to compare them fairly.
Sort things by temperature into hot, warm, and cold.
Match the right tool to the job: balance scale, measuring cup, ruler, thermometer.
Understand that bigger does not always mean heavier.
Recognise coins of different values and pay the exact price for something, using the fewest coins possible.

concepts.title: Mass — Heavier and Lighter
concepts.explanation: Mass is how heavy something is – how much ‘stuff’ is packed inside it. You compare two objects and says which is heavier, which is lighter, or whether they are the same. The best tool you own is your own two hands: hold one object in each hand and feel which pulls down more. How to teach it: Give you a stone in one hand and a leaf in the other. Ask, ‘Which hand feels heavier?’ Let them feel it, then say the sentence together: ‘The stone is heavier than the leaf. The leaf is lighter than the stone.’ Repeat with many pairs – a shoe and a spoon, a full cup and an empty cup, a book and a date. Always say both sentences so you hear that heavier and lighter are two ways of describing the same comparison. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Hold the stone in this hand and the date in that hand. Close your eyes and feel.” You: “Which one pulls your hand down more?” Child: “The stone.” You: “Yes! The stone is heavier than the date. So the date is lighter than the stone.” The most important idea in this concept is that bigger does not always mean heavier. A big puffed-up bag of crisps is lighter than a small stone; a large empty box is lighter than a small full cup. Children very often think the bigger thing must weigh more, so plan a surprise: let them lift a large light thing and a small heavy thing and feel that their guess was wrong. That moment of surprise teaches more than any rule.
concepts.example: Now bring in a balance scale so the comparison becomes something you can see, not just feel. Tie a cup to each end of a coat hanger, or balance a ruler across a pencil. Put a stone in one cup and a date in the other. The heavier side dips down; the lighter side lifts up. If the two sides sit level, the objects have the same mass. Predict which way it will tip before you let go – predicting then checking is where the real learning happens.

concepts.title: Balancing and Non-Standard Units
concepts.explanation: Once you understand ‘the heavy side goes down’, the balance becomes a way to measure mass using a non-standard unit. Instead of a number on a scale, we ask: ‘How many stones balance the mug?’ Put the mug in one cup and add stones to the other, one at a time, until the two sides sit level. How to teach it: Say, ‘Let us find how many stones are as heavy as this mug.’ Drop stones in one by one, counting together, until the scale balances. ‘Four stones balance the mug – so the mug has the same mass as 4 stones.’ Then try a heavier object and notice it needs more stones. This quietly links measuring back to counting, which you already knows well, and it shows that a heavier object needs more units to balance it.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us balance the cup with stones. Watch the sides.” You and child: “One stone… two… three… four. It is level now!” You: “The cup has the same mass as four stones. If we used a bigger cup, would we need more stones or fewer?” Child: “More!”

concepts.title: Capacity — Full, Empty, Holds More
concepts.explanation: Capacity is how much a container can hold inside. It is about the space inside a cup, jug, bottle, or bowl. The comparing words are holds more and holds less, and the state words are full, empty, nearly full, and nearly empty. How to teach it: Use water at wudu time or dry rice at home. Fill a small cup right up – ‘This cup is full.’ Tip it out – ‘Now it is empty.’ Then compare two containers by pouring: fill the cup and pour it into the jug. If the jug is not full yet, the jug holds more than the cup. Pour again and again; pouring is the whole lesson. Count how many little cups it takes to fill the big jug – this is capacity measured in a non-standard unit, just like weighing with stones. Guard against the most common muddle here: the difference between how much a container can hold and how much is in it right now. A big empty bottle still has a big capacity even though nothing is inside; a tiny full cup holds only a little even though it is full to the top. Keep the language clear – say ‘holds more’ for capacity, and ‘has more in it’ for the amount currently inside – and show both with real containers. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Fill the little cup with rice and pour it into the big jug. Is the jug full yet?” Child: “No.” You: “So the jug holds more than the cup. Let us count how many cups fill the jug.” You and child: “One cup… two cups… three cups. Three cups fill the jug!”
concepts.example: A lovely puzzle from the source book: mixing amounts. Show that a nearly empty jug poured together with a nearly full jug makes about one full jug. Pour two part-full cups into one and see the level rise. This gentle play with full, nearly full, nearly empty and empty builds a strong feel for capacity long before any measuring numbers appear.

concepts.title: Length and Height — Longer, Shorter, Taller
concepts.explanation: Length tells us how long or short something is; height tells us how tall something is when it stands up. You compare two objects and says which is longer, shorter, taller, or the same length. How to teach it: The golden rule is line objects up at one end. Put two pencils side by side with their bottoms level, then see which one sticks out further at the top – that one is longer. If you do not line them up fairly, a shorter pencil can look longer just because it is placed higher. Practise this fair-comparison habit every time, because it matters far more than the answer itself. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Put both pencils flat, with their ends touching this line. Now look at the tops.” You: “Which pencil reaches further?” Child: “This one.” You: “Yes — it is longer. The other one is shorter. We lined them up so it is a fair test.”
concepts.example: Also measure with non-standard units – how many hand-spans long is the mat? How many footsteps across the room? How many dates laid end to end is as long as the spoon? Counting units to measure length links straight back to counting stones on the balance and cups into the jug, so you see that all measuring is really careful comparing and counting. Compare heights too: stand two children back to back, or notice that the date palm is taller than the doorway.

concepts.title: Temperature — Hot, Warm, Cold
concepts.explanation: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. At this age we use only the feeling words – hot, warm, cool, cold – not degrees. You sort everyday things into these groups and learns that temperature helps us choose what to wear, eat, and drink. How to teach it: At wudu or washing time, set out water that is safely cold, gently warm, and cool. Feel each and name it. Then play a sorting game with familiar things: hot (the sun, hot soup, a cooking pot, fresh anjero), warm (bath water, camel milk, a sunny room), cold (ice, cold water, the night air, snow in pictures). Introduce the thermometer simply as ‘the tool grown-ups use to measure hot and cold’, without any numbers. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Feel this water. Is it hot, warm, or cold?” Child: “Warm.” You: “Good. Now think of hot soup at iftar — is that hot, warm, or cold?” Child: “Hot!” You: “And an ice cube?” Child: “Cold!” You: “You are sorting temperatures beautifully.”
concepts.example: Always weave in safety. Some hot things can burn – a cooking pot, hot oil, boiling water – so the rule is to look and ask a grown-up before touching, never to test hot things by grabbing. Talk about how we stay comfortable: a warm shawl when the desert night is cold, shade and cool water when the sun is hot. This links the maths of temperature to your real daily life.

concepts.title: Choosing the Right Tool
concepts.explanation: Finally, you learn that different questions need different tools. This ties the whole unit together: balance scale for mass, measuring cup or jug for capacity, ruler for length, thermometer for temperature. How to teach it: Lay out the four tools (or their pictures) and name each with its job. Then play a matching game: ‘How heavy is the bag of flour?’ → balance scale. ‘How much water is in the bottle?’ → measuring cup. ‘How long is the snake?’ → ruler. ‘How hot is the soup?’ → thermometer. Ask ‘why’ each time so you reason about which tool fits, rather than guessing. Thinking bigger always means heavier. Lift a large light thing and a small heavy thing to feel that this is not true. Confusing capacity with the amount inside. A big empty bottle still holds a lot; a small full cup holds little. Say ‘holds more’ for capacity and ‘has more in it’ for the amount. Not lining objects up when comparing length. A shorter object placed higher can look longer. Always line up one end for a fair test. Thinking tall means heavy. A tall thin stick can be lighter than a small stone. Height and mass are different things.
concepts.example: Reading the balance backwards. Remember the side that goes down is the heavier one.

concepts.title: Money — Coins and Paying the Exact Amount
concepts.explanation: Coins are a special kind of counting object: each coin stands for an amount, and different coins can be worth different amounts. Learning to recognise coins and pay the exact amount is an important, very real-life skill. How to teach it: Gather real coins if you have them, or make simple paper 'coins' labelled 1, 5, 10 and 20 shillings. Hold each coin and say its value aloud. Set up a tiny pretend shop with two or three items and a price label on each, such as a toy priced at 10 shillings. Pay the exact price using the coins in front of them — for example, one 10-shilling coin, or two 5-shilling coins, or ten 1-shilling coins. Talk about paying with the fewest coins possible: 'Instead of ten 1-shilling coins, one 10-shilling coin pays the same amount and is easier to carry.' Practise several different prices so you see that the same amount can often be paid in more than one way, just like with number bonds.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “This toy costs 10 shillings. Here are two 5-shilling coins and one 10-shilling coin. Which coins pay the exact price?” Child: “The two 5-shilling coins — 5 and 5 makes 10!” You: “Yes! And the one 10-shilling coin pays exactly 10 as well. Both ways are correct, but which uses fewer coins?” Child: “The one 10-shilling coin.”

explorations.title: Mass — Heavier and Lighter
explorations.context: Mass is how heavy something is – how much ‘stuff’ is packed inside it. You compare two objects and says which is heavier, which is lighter, or whether they are the same.
explorations.prompt: Hold a stone in one hand and a leaf in the other. Which one is heavier?
explorations.answer: The stone is heavier; the leaf is lighter.
explorations.hint: Feel which hand is pulled down more — that object is heavier.
explorations.explanation: Holding one object in each hand and feeling which one pulls down harder is your own built-in balance scale, and it is more reliable than judging by eye, since a bigger object is not always the heavier one. Say the comparison sentence together every time — 'the stone is heavier than the leaf' — so the vocabulary sticks alongside the physical feeling.

explorations.title: Balancing and Non-Standard Units
explorations.context: Once you understand ‘the heavy side goes down’, the balance becomes a way to measure mass using a non-standard unit.
explorations.prompt: You add stones one at a time to balance a mug, and the scale becomes level after 4 stones. How many stones balance the mug?
explorations.hint: Count the stones aloud as you add them, and stop once both sides sit level.
explorations.explanation: Once you accept that the heavier side of a scale always goes down, stones become a way to measure mass without needing any numbers on a dial — counting how many stones it takes to make both sides level tells you the object's mass in stones. A bigger object will always need more stones to balance it, which quietly previews the idea of measuring in units.

explorations.title: Capacity — Full, Empty, Holds More
explorations.context: Capacity is how much a container can hold inside. It is about the space inside a cup, jug, bottle, or bowl. The comparing words are holds more and holds less, and the state words are full, empty, nearly full, and nearly empty.
explorations.prompt: You pour a full cup of water into a jug, and the jug is still not full. Does the jug hold more or less than the cup?
explorations.answer: The jug holds more than the cup.
explorations.hint: Think about whether there is still room left in the jug after pouring.
explorations.explanation: Pouring a full container into another one and watching whether it overflows or leaves room is the fair test for 'holds more' or 'holds less' — guessing from the outside shape is unreliable, because a short wide jug can easily hold more than a tall thin bottle. Keep the two ideas separate: capacity is how much a container can hold, while full or empty describes how much is inside it right now.

explorations.title: Length and Height — Longer, Shorter, Taller
explorations.context: Length tells us how long or short something is; height tells us how tall something is when it stands up. You compare two objects and says which is longer, shorter, taller, or the same length.
explorations.prompt: Before comparing two pencils to see which is longer, what should you do first?
explorations.hint: Remember the golden rule for a fair comparison — start both objects from the same line.
explorations.explanation: Lining two objects up at one end before comparing is the one habit that matters here, because a shorter object placed higher up can trick the eye into looking longer. Once both objects start from the same line, whichever one reaches further really is the longer, or taller, one.

explorations.title: Temperature — Hot, Warm, Cold
explorations.context: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. At this age we use only the feeling words – hot, warm, cool, cold – not degrees. You sort everyday things into these groups and learns that temperature helps us choose what to wear, eat, and drink.
explorations.prompt: Is hot soup hot, warm, or cold?
explorations.hint: Think about how it feels fresh off the stove, before it cools down.
explorations.explanation: At this age, feeling words like hot, warm, cool and cold are what matter, not numbers on a thermometer — touch safely, or picture, familiar things like hot soup, bath water and an ice cube, and sort them by feel. Talking about why we choose warm clothes in the cold or shade in the heat links this new vocabulary to decisions you already makes every day.

explorations.title: Choosing the Right Tool
explorations.context: Finally, you learn that different questions need different tools. This ties the whole unit together: balance scale for mass, measuring cup or jug for capacity, ruler for length, thermometer for temperature.
explorations.prompt: Which tool would you use to find out how heavy a bag of flour is?
explorations.hint: Think about which of the four tools answers the question 'how heavy?'
explorations.explanation: Each question in this unit has one matching tool — a balance scale answers 'how heavy', a measuring cup or jug answers 'how much', a ruler answers 'how long', and a thermometer answers 'how hot' — so the real skill is spotting which question is being asked before reaching for a tool. Asking 'why that tool and not another' turns this into more than a matching game; it shows you that measuring always starts with understanding what you are trying to find out.

methods.title: How to Compare Two Objects by Mass
methods.example: Compare a stone and a leaf by holding one in each hand, then check with a balance scale.
steps: Hold one object in each hand and feel which one pulls your hand down more — that object is heavier.
Say the sentence together: 'The stone is heavier than the leaf. The leaf is lighter than the stone.'
Check the guess on a balance scale — the pan that goes down holds the heavier object.

methods.title: How to Balance an Object Using Stones
methods.example: Find out how many stones balance a mug by adding stones to the other side of the scale.
steps: Put the object, for example a mug, into one pan of the balance scale.
Add stones one at a time to the other pan, counting aloud each time a stone is added.
Stop once both pans sit level, then count the stones — that number is the object's mass in stones.

methods.title: How to Compare Capacity by Pouring
methods.example: Pour water from a full cup into an empty jug to see which container holds more.
steps: Fill the first container right to the top and say, 'This is full.'
Pour all of the water from the first container into the second container.
If the second container is not full yet, it holds more; if the water overflows, it holds less.

methods.title: How to Decide Which of Two Objects Is Heavier
methods.example: Look at a shoe and a sock and work out which one is heavier before circling it.
steps: Picture holding the shoe in one hand and the sock in the other hand.
Decide which one would pull the hand down more — that is the heavier object.
Circle the heavier object on the page, and say why: 'The shoe is heavier because it is made of harder, thicker material.'

methods.title: How to Compare Very Different-Sized Animals by Mass
methods.example: Compare an elephant and a mouse to see that a much bigger animal is also much heavier.
steps: Look at the two animals and notice how much bigger the elephant is than the mouse.
Explain that a bigger body usually has more 'stuff' packed inside, so it usually weighs more.
Circle the elephant as the heavier animal, and say: 'The mouse is much lighter than the elephant.'

methods.title: How to Compare a Book and a Feather by Mass
methods.example: Compare a book and a feather to learn that looking big does not always mean being heavy.
steps: Notice that the feather can look large and fluffy, while the book looks smaller and flat.
Imagine holding both in your hands — the feather barely presses down, but the book presses down hard.
Circle the book as the heavier object, and remember: bigger does not always mean heavier.

workedExamples.title: Comparing a Stone and a Leaf by Mass
workedExamples.prompt: Hold a small stone in one hand and a dry leaf in the other. Which one is heavier?
workedExamples.solution: Say to you: 'Close your eyes and feel both hands.' The stone pulls the hand down more, so the stone is heavier. The leaf barely presses on the hand, so the leaf is lighter. Say together: 'The stone is heavier than the leaf. The leaf is lighter than the stone.'

workedExamples.title: Balancing a Mug with Stones
workedExamples.prompt: Put a mug on one side of a balance scale. Add stones to the other side, one at a time, until the scale is level. How many stones balance the mug?
workedExamples.solution: Add stones one by one while counting aloud: one, two, three, four. When the scale sits level on four stones, say: 'Four stones balance the mug, so the mug has the same mass as four stones.' A bigger mug would need more stones to balance it.

workedExamples.title: Comparing a Cup and a Jug by Capacity
workedExamples.prompt: Fill a small cup to the top with water, then pour it into an empty jug. Does the jug hold more or less than the cup?
workedExamples.solution: Fill the cup right up and say, 'This cup is full.' Pour all of the water into the jug. If the water only fills part of the jug, the jug holds more than the cup. If the water overflows the jug, the jug holds less than the cup.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Heavier Object: Shoe or Sock
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a picture of a shoe and a sock. Circle the one that is heavier.
workedExamples.solution: Imagine holding the shoe in one hand and the sock in the other. The shoe is made of thicker, harder material, so it pulls the hand down more. Circle the shoe, because the shoe is heavier than the sock.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Heavier Animal: Elephant or Mouse
workedExamples.prompt: 🐘 elephant 🐁 mouse — circle the one that is heavier.
workedExamples.solution: The elephant is enormous and the mouse is tiny, so the elephant has far more mass. Circle the elephant, because the elephant is heavier and the mouse is much lighter.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Heavier Object: Book or Feather
workedExamples.prompt: 📕 book 🪶 feather — circle the one that is heavier.
workedExamples.solution: A feather looks big and fluffy, but there is almost nothing packed inside it. The book is full of paper, so it is heavier even though the feather might look larger. Circle the book, because the book is heavier and the feather is lighter.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Heavier Vehicle: Car or Bicycle
workedExamples.prompt: 🚗 car 🚲 bicycle — circle the one that is heavier.
workedExamples.solution: A car is built from a lot of metal and is much bigger than a bicycle, so it has far more mass. Circle the car, because the car is heavier and the bicycle is lighter.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Container That Holds More: Bucket or Bowl
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a picture of a bucket and a bowl. Circle the one that holds more.
workedExamples.solution: Picture pouring water from the bucket into the bowl — the bowl would overflow long before the bucket is empty. Circle the bucket, because the bucket holds more than the bowl and the bowl holds less.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Container That Holds More: Spoon or Cup
workedExamples.prompt: 🥄 spoon ☕ cup — circle the one that holds more.
workedExamples.solution: A spoon can only hold a tiny amount of liquid before it spills, but a cup can hold much more. Circle the cup, because the cup holds more than the spoon and the spoon holds less.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Container That Holds More: Bathtub or Sink
workedExamples.prompt: 🛁 bathtub 🚰 sink — circle the one that holds more.
workedExamples.solution: A bathtub is large enough for a child to sit inside, while a sink is small and only used for washing hands. Circle the bathtub, because the bathtub holds more than the sink and the sink holds less.

workedExamples.title: Circling the Container That Holds More: Jug or Tiny Cup
workedExamples.prompt: 🫙 jug 🥃 tiny cup — circle the one that holds more.
workedExamples.solution: The jug is tall and wide, while the tiny cup could be filled and emptied into the jug many times before the jug is full. Circle the jug, because the jug holds more than the tiny cup and the tiny cup holds less.

workedExamples.title: Finding the Longest Pencil and the Tallest Child
workedExamples.prompt: Three pencils are placed with their bottoms lined up on a table. Pencil A's tip reaches highest. Which pencil is the longest?
workedExamples.solution: Because all three pencils are lined up fairly at one end, the pencil whose tip reaches furthest is the longest — that is Pencil A. The same idea works for height: if two children stand back to back on flat ground, the one whose head reaches higher is the taller child.

practice.prompt: You hold an orange in one hand and a small feather in the other. Which one is heavier?
practice.answer: The orange is heavier; the feather is lighter.
practice.hint: Feel which hand is pulled down more — that object is heavier.

practice.prompt: A mug is placed on one side of a balance scale. Stones are added to the other side until it is level, and you count 3 stones. How many stones balance the mug?
practice.hint: Count the stones one at a time until both sides sit level.

practice.prompt: You fill a bowl to the top with rice, then pour it into an empty pot and it only fills half the pot. Does the pot hold more or less than the bowl?
practice.answer: The pot holds more than the bowl.
practice.hint: Think about what happens when you pour a full container into another one.

practice.prompt: Which is heavier: a hammer or a balloon?
practice.answer: The hammer is heavier; the balloon is lighter.
practice.hint: A hammer is made of hard metal and wood; a balloon is mostly filled with air.

practice.answer: The elephant is heavier; the mouse is lighter.
practice.hint: Think about the size and how much 'stuff' is packed inside each animal.

practice.answer: The book is heavier; the feather is lighter, even though the feather can look bigger and fluffier.
practice.hint: Remember: looking big does not always mean being heavy.

practice.answer: The car is heavier; the bicycle is lighter.
practice.hint: Think about how much metal and material is packed into each one.

practice.prompt: Which holds more: a saucepan or a mug?
practice.answer: The saucepan holds more; the mug holds less.
practice.hint: Imagine pouring water from the saucepan into the mug — would the mug overflow?

practice.answer: The cup holds more; the spoon holds less.
practice.hint: A spoon only holds a tiny amount before it spills.

practice.prompt: 🛁 bathtub 🚰 sink — which holds more water?
practice.answer: The bathtub holds more; the sink holds less.
practice.hint: Think about which one you could fit inside.

practice.prompt: 🫙 jug 🥃 tiny cup — which holds more?
practice.answer: The jug holds more; the tiny cup holds less.
practice.hint: Think about how many times you could fill the tiny cup from the jug.

practice.prompt: Two ribbons are lined up at one end on the table. Ribbon A reaches further than Ribbon B. Which ribbon is longer?
practice.answer: Ribbon A is longer; Ribbon B is shorter.
practice.hint: Remember the golden rule: line objects up fairly at one end before comparing.

rules.title: Bigger Does Not Always Mean Heavier
rules.text: The most important idea in this concept is that bigger does not always mean heavier. A big puffed-up bag of crisps is lighter than a small stone; a large empty box is lighter than a small full cup. Children very often think the bigger thing must weigh more, so plan a surprise: let them lift a large light thing and a small heavy thing and feel that their guess was wrong. That moment of surprise teaches more than any rule.

rules.title: How to Teach It: The Golden Rule for Comparing Length
rules.text: How to teach it: The golden rule is line objects up at one end. Put two pencils side by side with their bottoms level, then see which one sticks out further at the top – that one is longer. If you do not line them up fairly, a shorter pencil can look longer just because it is placed higher. Practise this fair-comparison habit every time, because it matters far more than the answer itself.

rules.title: Safety First: Hot Things Can Burn
rules.text: Always weave in safety. Some hot things can burn – a cooking pot, hot oil, boiling water – so the rule is to look and ask a grown-up before touching, never to test hot things by grabbing. Talk about how we stay comfortable: a warm shawl when the desert night is cold, shade and cool water when the sun is hot. This links the maths of temperature to your real daily life.

terms: Has more mass / has less mass
A tool that tips down on the heavier side
Two things that weigh the same
How much a container can hold inside
commonMistakes: A common mistake is to think the sink holds more because it is used more often during the day
Remember that how often something is used has nothing to do with its capacity — size and depth decide who holds more.
A common mistake is to think one tiny cup could hold as much as the jug because both are 'containers'
Remember that the jug can refill many tiny cups, so it clearly holds far more.
A common mistake is to think emptying speed depends only on the size of the hole, not the amount of water
Remember that the bathtub simply has more water in it, so even at the same pouring speed it takes longer.
A common mistake is to think the answer is 'the same' because both are used to hold the same juice
Remember that capacity is compared by how much fits inside, and one jug clearly fits more than one tiny cup.
A common mistake is to think the bigger, fluffier cotton ball must be heavier
Remember to feel both hands: the rock pulls down more, so the rock is heavier and the cotton ball is lighter.

fluency.prompt: You hold a small rock in one hand and a cotton ball in the other. Which one is lighter?
fluency.answer: The cotton ball is lighter; the rock is heavier.
fluency.hint: Feel which hand is pulled down less — that object is lighter.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think the bigger, fluffier cotton ball must be heavier. Remember to feel both hands: the rock pulls down more, so the rock is heavier and the cotton ball is lighter.

fluency.prompt: A cup is placed on one side of a balance scale. You add stones one at a time and the scale becomes level after 5 stones. How many stones balance the cup?
fluency.hint: Count the stones aloud as you add them, and stop when the scale is level.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to stop counting too early, before the scale is truly level. Check that both sides sit flat and even before giving the final stone count.

fluency.prompt: You pour a full cup of water into an empty bowl and the bowl is still not full. Does the bowl hold more or less than the cup?
fluency.answer: The bowl holds more than the cup.
fluency.hint: Think about whether the second container overflowed or still had room left.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to say the bowl holds less just because it looks flatter than the cup. Focus on whether the poured water filled it up or left room — here there was room left, so the bowl holds more.

fluency.prompt: Which is heavier: a brick or a sponge?
fluency.answer: The brick is heavier; the sponge is lighter.
fluency.hint: Think about which one is solid and hard, and which one is soft and full of air holes.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think a bigger sponge could be heavier than a smaller brick. Remember that a sponge is full of tiny air holes, so it stays light no matter its size.

fluency.answer: The mouse is lighter; the elephant is heavier.
fluency.hint: Think about which animal has less 'stuff' packed inside its body.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to only think about height and forget mass. Even a tall thin animal could be lighter than a short heavy one, but here the tiny mouse is clearly lighter than the huge elephant.

fluency.answer: The feather is lighter; the book is heavier.
fluency.hint: Remember: something that looks big and fluffy can still be very light.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to say the feather is heavier because it can look larger floating in the air. Remember to imagine holding both in their hands — the feather barely presses down at all.

fluency.answer: The bicycle is lighter; the car is heavier.
fluency.hint: Think about how much metal is used to build each one.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to compare only length or size, since a car and a long bicycle can look similar from some angles. Focus on mass: the car is packed with far more metal, so it is heavier.

fluency.prompt: Which holds more: a flask or an eggcup?
fluency.answer: The flask holds more; the eggcup holds less.
fluency.hint: Imagine pouring the flask's water into the eggcup — would it overflow?
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to judge by height alone and ignore width. Even a short wide flask can hold more than a tall thin eggcup — always imagine pouring one into the other to check.

fluency.answer: The spoon holds less; the cup holds more.
fluency.hint: Think about which one would spill first if you kept pouring water in.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to confuse 'holds less' with 'is smaller in every way'. Here it is simply about capacity: the spoon's small bowl overflows almost immediately, so it holds less.

fluency.prompt: 🛁 bathtub 🚰 sink — which holds less water?
fluency.answer: The sink holds less; the bathtub holds more.
fluency.hint: Think about which one you use just for washing your hands.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think they hold about the same because both are used with water in the bathroom. Remember that a whole child can sit inside a bathtub but not inside a sink, so the bathtub holds far more.

fluency.prompt: 🫙 jug 🥃 tiny cup — which holds less?
fluency.answer: The tiny cup holds less; the jug holds more.
fluency.hint: Think about how many tiny cups of water it would take to fill the jug.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think the tiny cup holds more because it is easier to carry. Remember that ease of carrying is about mass, not capacity — the jug clearly holds more liquid.

fluency.prompt: Two ropes are lined up at one end. Rope A's other end reaches further than Rope B's. Which rope is shorter?
fluency.answer: Rope B is shorter; Rope A is longer.
fluency.hint: Look at which end reaches less far once both ropes are lined up fairly.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to compare the ropes without lining up their ends first, which can make a shorter rope look longer. Always line them up fairly at one end before deciding.

realProblems.prompt: At home, your family fills the bathtub for a bath and the sink for washing hands. Which one holds more water?
realProblems.answer: The bathtub holds more water than the sink.
realProblems.hint: Think about which one is big enough to sit inside.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think the sink holds more because it is used more often during the day. Remember that how often something is used has nothing to do with its capacity — size and depth decide who holds more.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a seller pours milk from a big jug into tiny cups for customers. Which holds more: the jug or one tiny cup?
realProblems.answer: The jug holds more than one tiny cup.
realProblems.hint: Think about how many tiny cups the seller can fill from just one jug.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think one tiny cup could hold as much as the jug because both are 'containers'. Remember that the jug can refill many tiny cups, so it clearly holds far more.

realProblems.prompt: On a journey, you compare two walking sticks by standing them up next to each other on the ground. One reaches higher than the other. Which stick is taller?
realProblems.answer: The stick that reaches higher is the taller one.
realProblems.hint: Make sure both sticks are standing on the same flat ground before comparing.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to compare the sticks while one is leaning and one is standing straight, which makes the leaning one look shorter than it really is. Always stand both up straight on the same flat surface first.

realProblems.prompt: Every evening, you empty a small basin used for washing feet and a large bathtub used for bathing. Which one takes longer to empty: the basin or the bathtub?
realProblems.answer: The bathtub takes longer to empty, because it holds more water than the basin.
realProblems.hint: Think about which container has more water inside it to begin with.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think emptying speed depends only on the size of the hole, not the amount of water. Remember that the bathtub simply has more water in it, so even at the same pouring speed it takes longer.

realProblems.prompt: At home you use a jug to fill several tiny cups with juice for the whole family. If one jug fills 6 tiny cups exactly, does the jug hold more or less than one tiny cup?
realProblems.answer: The jug holds more than one tiny cup — enough to fill 6 of them.
realProblems.hint: Think about how many tiny cups you counted the jug being able to fill.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to think the answer is 'the same' because both are used to hold the same juice. Remember that capacity is compared by how much fits inside, and one jug clearly fits more than one tiny cup.

realProblems.prompt: You and your younger sibling stand back to back on the same flat floor to see who is taller. Your head reaches higher. Who is taller?
realProblems.answer: You are taller than your younger sibling.
realProblems.hint: Make sure you are both standing up straight on the same flat floor before comparing.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A common mistake is to compare heights while one child is on tiptoes or standing on a step, which unfairly makes them look taller. Always compare on the same flat floor, standing normally.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A car and a bicycle are placed on a balance scale. Explain how you would know which one is heavier, and what the balance scale would show.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: You put the car on one side of the balance scale and the bicycle on the other. Because the car has far more mass than the bicycle, the car's side goes down and the bicycle's side goes up. This shows the car is heavier and the bicycle is lighter — the balance scale always tips down on the side with the heavier object.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two bags of flour are placed on a balance scale and it stays level, with neither side going down. Explain what this tells us about the two bags.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: When the balance scale stays level with neither side going down, it means both sides are pulling down by the same amount. This tells us the two bags of flour have the same mass — neither bag is heavier or lighter than the other.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A cup of water and a cup of sand look different, but a balance scale shows they have the same mass. Explain how this is different from asking which cup holds more water.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The balance scale only tells us about mass — how heavy each cup is — and here it shows both cups pull down by the same amount, so they have the same mass. This is a different question from capacity, which is about how much a container can hold inside. Two containers can have the same mass but hold different amounts, or hold the same amount but have different masses, so each must be checked separately.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Length and Height — Longer, Shorter, Taller.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Length tells us how long or short something is; height tells us how tall something is when it stands up. You compare two objects and says which is longer, shorter, taller, or the same length. How to teach it: The golden rule is line objects up at one end. Put two pencils side by side with their bottoms level, then see which one sticks out further at the top – that one is longer. If you do not line them up fairly, a shorter pencil can look longer just because it is placed higher. Practise this fair-comparison habit every time, because it matters far more than the answer itself.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Temperature — Hot, Warm, Cold.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. At this age we use only the feeling words – hot, warm, cool, cold – not degrees. You sort everyday things into these groups and learns that temperature helps us choose what to wear, eat, and drink. How to teach it: At wudu or washing time, set out water that is safely cold, gently warm, and cool. Feel each and name it. Then play a sorting game with familiar things: hot (the sun, hot soup, a cooking pot, fresh anjero), warm (bath water, camel milk, a sunny room), cold (ice, cold water, the night air, snow in pictures). Introduce the thermometer simply as ‘the tool grown-ups use to measure hot and cold’, without any numbers.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Choosing the Right Tool.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Finally, you learn that different questions need different tools. This ties the whole unit together: balance scale for mass, measuring cup or jug for capacity, ruler for length, thermometer for temperature. How to teach it: Lay out the four tools (or their pictures) and name each with its job. Then play a matching game: ‘How heavy is the bag of flour?’ → balance scale. ‘How much water is in the bottle?’ → measuring cup. ‘How long is the snake?’ → ruler. ‘How hot is the soup?’ → thermometer. Ask ‘why’ each time so you reason about which tool fits, rather than guessing.
